extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, literary critics, authors and playwrights (early-18th-century readership interested in poetry, theatre, and manners)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive critical guidance on writing and judging poetry and plays, and on social conduct/education (fine breeding, mourning, manners) as addressed to readers, authors, and parents. The page gives standards for what counts as good wit, good poetry, good theatrical characterisation, and proper social behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of Thought and Words
rubrics_metrics.description: If Wit is defined as a Propriety of Thoughts and Words, the definition extends to all sorts of Poetry: 'Propriety of Thought is that Fancy which arises naturally from the Subject, or which the Poet adapts to it. Propriety of Words is the cloathing of these Thoughts with such Expressions as are naturally proper to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to every poem: thoughts must arise naturally from the subject; choose words that are naturally proper to those thoughts. (Footnote referencing Dryden's Preface to 'Albion and Albanius'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as the foundation of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is the first Quality, and, as it were, the foundation of Thought; without truth, apparent beauty of thought is faulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some critics argue falsehood can give grace (e.g., in epigrams), the general rule is to prefer truth as the basis for witty and critical thinking. (Summarised from Bouhours: 'Truth is the first Quality...')

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor classical Simplicity over 'Gothick' Extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: Good poetry and taste aim for the 'beautiful Simplicity of the old Greeks and Romans' rather than the extravagancies of an irregular fancy (the 'Goths' in Poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overornamented, irregular, fanciful devices that substitute for classical simplicity and clarity; seek naturalness and measured expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and Improvement on Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should not merely borrow from a greater master without adding improvement; copying without original contribution is seen as failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden's criticism of Ovid: borrowing the same subject from a superior master and 'improving nothing' is evidence of lack of nature and recourse to mere witticisms. Strive to bring something new or to genuinely improve what is borrowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit arises from Resemblance and Opposition of Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the resemblance and the opposition of ideas often produce Wit, e.g., in turns, antitheses, and pointed contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural analogies and contrasts to generate wit; these are fruitful sources for cleverness when grounded in truth and propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid catering only to 'Les Petits Esprits' (mob readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a class of readers who prefer 'the Husk and Rind of Wit' — quibbles, conceits, epigrams — over solid sense and elegant expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should not write merely to please this loud, numerous class; instead encourage readers to improve by offering sound writing and fostering conversation with men of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject mechanical/contrived devices as substitutes for true Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Games and artifices (anagrams, acrosticks, chronograms, lipograms, rebuses, crambo, puns/double rhymes and other verbal tricks) are shown as the amusements of 'False Wit' rather than genuine poetic wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute contrivance and puzzle-like cleverness for natural, meaningful wit; such devices often produce laughter but lack substance and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure plays by Reason, Truth, and Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason, Truth, and Nature are the measures of praise and dispraise for theatrical works; general opinion is secondary to these standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a play, ask whether it accords with reason, truthful representation, and natural human behaviour; these should trump popularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation: Fine Gentleman should be honest and refined
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'fine gentleman' — as a character-type — ought to be honest in actions and refined in language; coarse vice or clownish speech do not make a proper gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid portraying gallantry as a cover for knavery or making vice appear as merit; virtuous behaviour and refined expression should underpin celebrated characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not celebrate vice or corrupt nature as merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Works which represent corruption, degeneracy, or the ruin of virtue as objects of applause are flawed: nature in its corruption is not to be the standard of admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about plays/comedy that derive humour or reputation from immoral conduct; such works may well depict life but should not be celebrated as exemplars of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre's social responsibility: avoid promoting bad manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of wit in the theatre significantly affects the manners of gentlemen; therefore theatrical wit should be judged by its influence on public behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and critics should consider how theatrical portrayals shape manners — prefer works that cultivate good sense and virtue rather than encourage folly or indecency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance mind and body in education (Fine Breeding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents often overvalue the adorning of the person for daughters and the embellishment of the mind for sons; the true art is to improve mind and body together so that gesture follows thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In educating young women (and children generally), pursue a middle way: teach bodily grace (walking, carriage, comportment) but pair it with cultivation of the mind so behaviour expresses virtue and thought, not mere affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Good Breeding (genuine) over Fine Breeding (affectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Breeding is plain, genuine behaviour rooted in sense; Fine Breeding can become a superficial, fantastical gravity of manner that produces coquets and affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for natural modesty and simplicity rather than forced 'fine' gestures and artificial poses; avoid teaching children to sigh, smile, or walk only as practiced affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gesture should follow Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The true art is 'to make Gesture follow Thought' — physical carriage and motion should express inner virtues and understanding, not precede or fake them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate inward character and understanding first, then allow outward manners to arise naturally; avoid training gestures in absence of corresponding thought and mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in public ceremonies (mourning) and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: The fashion of mourning, when adopted as a mere external ceremony by those not truly sorrowful, degenerates into absurdity and economic harm; public honours should be restrained to those properly related or affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive, performative public ceremonies that impoverish dependents (e.g., mercers, milliners) or blur distinctions of genuine mourning; honours and ceremonial mourning should be appropriate and limited to those with a legitimate claim.
